text.title: Constitution.md Core Rules
text.summary: Seven testable rules governing the file, not its content. R1 is the admission gate; R2 is the cap that makes the file loadable; R7 is the delegation that stops it swallowing the domain.

rule.statement: A candidate rule is admitted ONLY if all four hold. **Durable** — it outlives the current feature; anything true only for the sprint in progress is a task note. **Cross-cutting** — it constrains more than one feature or more than one layer; a rule touching one module belongs in that module's `AGENTS.md`. **Contestable** — a competent engineer could have chosen otherwise; "write tests" is not contestable and therefore carries no information. **Checkable** — a reviewer can name the observation that would show it was violated. A candidate failing any part MUST be routed, not softened: domain facts and data model to `project-spec/`, outcomes and metrics to `roadmap.md`, the reasoning behind a single choice to `decisions.md` or an ADR, module-local conventions to that module's `AGENTS.md`.
rule.rationale: The word `constitution` appears in 174 live files in this corpus as a concept and in exactly zero methodology slugs; `sdlc-ai/task-spec-kit-three-step` demands a Constitution Gate and never defines what passes it. An undefined gate is filled with whatever the author had open at the time, which is why real constitutions drift into framework versions and aspirations. The admission test is the definition that was missing.

rule.statement: The file MUST contain at most twenty rules, and each rule body MUST be at most sixty words excluding its why. Reaching the cap is not a signal to raise it: it is a signal to merge two rules, demote one to a module `AGENTS.md`, or retire one that no longer binds. The cap is a forcing constraint on the author, not a measured optimum, and MUST NOT be presented as an empirical finding in customer-facing copy.
rule.rationale: The cap exists to buy one property: the file is cheap enough that every phase — planning, execution, review, readiness — can load all of it, every time. A constitution that is loaded selectively is a constitution whose rules apply selectively, and an unread rule is not a rule. Twenty short rules is roughly the budget at which that property holds for every phase simultaneously; no measurement backs the specific number, and pretending otherwise would be the kind of unsourced claim this corpus is meant to avoid.

rule.statement: Every rule MUST carry exactly one sentence of why, and that sentence MUST be obtained BEFORE the rule text is drafted. In elicitation the question is "what have you had to explain twice?" — the answer is the why, and the rule is written from it. A rule whose why cannot be stated in one sentence is not yet understood well enough to bind anyone, and MUST be deferred rather than written with a placeholder reason.

rationale.source: practitioner rule — rule survival under pressure

rule.rationale: A rule without a reason is a preference, and a preference loses its first argument with a deadline. The ordering matters because a why written after the rule is a justification: it rationalises whatever was already decided and rules out nothing. A why written first is a constraint that the rule then has to satisfy, and it is also the only thing a reviewer can weigh when someone proposes an exception.

rule.statement: Rules MUST carry stable identifiers of the form `R-NN`, numbered sequentially from `R-01`, unique within the file, and never reused. Retiring a rule removes it from the standing set; the id is retired with it and is not reissued to a new rule. Reordering the file MUST NOT renumber the rules.
rule.rationale: A review blocker that cites `R-07` is arguable — a reader can go and read `R-07`, and either the code violates it or the reviewer misread it. A blocker citing neither a `spec.md` line nor a constitution rule id is a nit, and nits are what turn reviews into taste arguments. Renumbering on reorder silently invalidates every citation ever written, including the ones in closed pull requests.

rule.statement: The file MUST contain a Compliance section naming, for the rule set as a whole, (a) who or what checks it — a reviewer, a CI job, a linter, an agent phase; (b) what happens when a violation is found; and (c) which rules are mechanically checked today versus checked only by reading. A rule that is mechanically checkable SHOULD be moved into the checker and cite it, so that the constitution shrinks as tooling grows.
rule.rationale: A rule with no named checker degrades into folklore within about a quarter, and the failure is silent: nobody announces that they stopped enforcing it. Splitting mechanically-checked from read-only rules is also honest — it tells the reader exactly how much confidence a green build buys, which is the difference between a gate and a ritual.

rule.statement: The file MUST carry a semver version, a ratification date and a last-amended date in a footer, and every change MUST update them: MAJOR when a rule is removed or its meaning is reversed, MINOR when a rule is added, PATCH for wording that does not change what is permitted. Every change MUST also update the Sync Impact Report comment at the top of the file, naming the version transition, the rules added, modified or removed, and any template or document now out of sync. A rule that no longer holds MUST be amended or retired — never left in place and quietly ignored, and never superseded by appending a contradicting rule below it.
rule.rationale: The constitution is the standing set; `decisions.md` and ADRs are the history. Conflating them produces the common failure where the file is append-only and contains two rules that contradict each other, at which point the reader picks whichever one supports their position. The Sync Impact Report exists because a rule change usually invalidates something downstream — a plan template, a review checklist — and nothing else in the repo will notice.

rule.statement: The Scope section MUST name the project's `project-spec/` location and state explicitly that domain facts, business rules, the data model, invariants and deploy topology live there and not here. Nothing whose truth depends on the product domain rather than on how the work is done may be admitted as a rule.

rationale.source: sdd/project-spec-structure; comparison against Spec Kit and Agent OS, 2026-08-04

rule.rationale: This is the single place this shape beats the framework constitutions it resembles: they have no second file to delegate to, so the domain leaks into the constitution and the file stops being loadable within a few months. Delegation keeps the constitution about *how the work is done* — which is stable — while the domain lives in a file built to be rewritten as the product is understood.
